articles.text: Current vote counts published by the Alameda County Registrar of Voters show Michael Malione, Max Roman, and Susy Struble have been elected to fouryear terms on Piedmont’s School Board. They were elected in the November General Election in a race not contested. All three candidates were on the ballot for the first time and enjoyed healthy leads over candidate Victoria Rosenbaum after she withdrew from the race and endorsed Malione, Roman and Struble. Approximately 5,500 Piedmont ballots have been counted of the 8,975 registered voters in the city. Many following school news may be surprised at how many votes Victoria Rosenbaum received even though she endorsed the other three candidates. The registrar’s office was unable to remove her name from the ballot prior to the election, and she has received 17% of the votes. The next round of results will be dropped on Friday, but regardless of tally finalities Malione, Roman and Struble will join the school board.

A post-election prayer By Pastor James Hopkins The political and religious circles I move in are generally center or left of center. Thus, I am in touch with a host of people who are very upset by many of the results of the 2024 elections. I hear their disappointment and feel their pain. I am also trying to find a way to remind myself, as well as my friends, that the purpose of our faith is not to win elections or gain political power. Our purpose is to love God with everything we have and to love our neighbors, even when we can think of many reasons not to. Winning elections and gaining political power may be a means by which we love our neighbors, but they are not, in and of themselves, our reason for being. In this vein, I find myself drawn to Psalm 146, verses 3-6 which read: 3 Do not put your trust in princes, in human beings, who cannot save. 4 When their spirit departs, they return to the ground; on that very day their plans come to nothing. 5 Blessed are those whose help is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the Lord their God. While the psalmist did not live in a democracy and thus did have the right to vote for political leaders, they were not a stranger to narratives that proclaimed the king to be divine or theologies that declared the king to be heaven sent. Thus, the words of the psalm are prophetic, “We refuse to entrust our ultimate well-being to any human ruler, as powerful as they may be. It is only the Creator of All to whom we turn for lasting help, enduring hope.” This is the prayer I offer in response to the prophetic theology of this enduring psalm. Creator of All: While, in these confusing days, we recognize the importance of government and those who govern, we also recognize that the well-being of our souls is in other hands, hands that are eternal, hands that embody steadfast love. Amen. I hope the prayer might be helpful to each of you in your work of loving God and neighbor. Rev. articles.text: The following letter was sent to Piedmont City Council on November 12. Editor: I live in the immediate vicinity of 29 Wildwood Avenue (site of the former Shell Station). I’m pleased about the overall direction of development; the EV hub is very promising. We appreciate the effort that Shell Oil and the Planning Commission have executed towards developing the plans. We are especially grateful for the Planning Commission resolution (not available yet, so relying on notes from the 10/28 meeting) which includes: Recommending the historical operating hours of 6am to 10pm • Requiring a written assessment of an underground vault for the electrical transformers (a one-time expense for the permanent benefit of reducing noise and EMF exposure) • Considering that the electrical transformers be at the furthest location from the residences rather than closest As a reminder to the Council, the consistent feedback from neighborhood residents has been very positive about the EV Hub itself but opposed to 24/7/365 operating hours as an attractive nuisance. Actual nuisance is when the site is used as intended, and it’s 3 am. Attractive nuisance is when the site is used for unintended purposes, again at 3 a.m. Shell has argued that CCTV and lighting will discourage the crime and nuisance elements. We agree, however 24/7 operation is not a prerequisite for CCTV and lighting. We are uneasy offering comments without the benefit of the resolutions from the October 28 Planning Commission meeting. We hope these will be faithfully represented by Staff recommendations and without any new information that has not yet been shared with the community. The immediate neighbors of this project, and the broader residents of Piedmont, rely on the Planning Commission and City Council for stewardship. You have the greatest influence and control over development at this site at this moment; there is no going back. Your active leadership and support for the above mitigations will make this project a success for everyone. –Miguel DeAvila For 25 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. articles.text: Piedmont is launching a Local Hazard Mitigation Plan update project to assess any changes to the hazards the city faces as well as recommend projects to reduce risk. This initiative, which formally kicks off next week, will study the specific ways Piedmont would likely be impacted by natural hazards like earthquakes, wildfires, and severe weather and develop a roadmap showing what can be done to reduce or avoid expected damages. Developing this plan and receiving approval from FEMA and Cal OES ensures Piedmont is eligible for state and federal disaster assistance and mitigation grants. Public participation is a key focus for the project, and there will be multiple opportunities for community members to help shape the plan over the next nine months. Subscribers to the project email list will be notified directly about upcoming meetings, events, and opportunities to provide input. Community members can learn more, offer comments, and connect with members of the project team at the following events: • Wednesday, November 13, 1-4 p.m. - Hazard Mitigation Planning Committee meeting at the Piedmont Veterans Memorial Building, 401 Highland Avenue • Sunday, November 17, 2-4:30 p.m. - Fire Department table at the Piedmont Adult Recreation Expo at the Piedmont Veterans Memorial Building, 401 Highland Avenue • Thursday, December 5, 5:30 p.m. - Public Safety Committee meeting at Piedmont City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue Residents can stay informed about the City’s Local Hazard Mitigation Plan update project by subscribing to project email updates at piedmont.ca.gov/ LHMPnews.

articles.text: For many, the idea of speech therapy conjures images of children learning to pronounce sounds correctly or overcome stutters. However, speech therapy is not just for kids—it plays a crucial role in helping adults navigate communication challenges as well. Whether due to injury, illness, or long-standing speech difficulties, adults can benefit greatly from speech therapy. This vital healthcare service is often underutilized by adults who may not realize how much it can improve their quality of life. Speech therapy for adults is designed to help individuals improve their communication abilities. This may involve refining articulation, enhancing fluency, or strengthening the muscles used for speech. In adults, therapy is often necessary after medical events such as strokes, traumatic brain injuries or concussions, or surgeries. Speech-language pathologists (SLPs), or speech therapists, also work with adults experiencing conditions like Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), which can impact both speech and swallowing functions. Some adults may have dealt with speech issues throughout their lives, such as stuttering or voice disorders. Others may struggle newly acquired communication issues, such as aphasia, a condition that affects language comprehension and production, often following a stroke or brain injury. In these cases, speech therapy helps restore communication skills, empowering individuals to regain independence and confidence. Adults seek speech therapy for many reasons, but the primary goal is always the same: to improve communication and quality of life. For those recovering from strokes, speech therapy can help them regain the ability to speak clearly, which is critical for reestablishing social connections and functioning in everyday life. In some cases, therapy may involve relearning how to speak entirely. Similarly, individuals with degenerative neurological diseases, such as Parkinson’s, often face challenges with speech volume, clarity, and swallowing. Therapy can slow the progression of these issues, giving patients more control over their speech for longer periods. Voice disorders, caused by vocal strain, injury, or surgery, are another reason adults turn to speech therapists. Teachers, singers, and public speakers are especially prone to vocal damage and may require therapy to heal and retrain their vocal cords. Speech difficulties can be deeply frustrating, leading to feelings of isolation, embarrassment, and low self-esteem. Many adults find themselves withdrawing from social situations or avoiding conversations because they fear being misunderstood. The emotional toll can be as significant as the physical challenges. Speech therapy provides not only practical tools but emotional support. As patients make progress, their confidence grows. The ability to communicate effectively – whether in personal relationships, at work, or in public – can transform a person’s outlook on life. The therapeutic process is also about building a new identity around a stronger, more capable voice. For adults facing speech and communication challenges, speech therapy offers a lifeline. It’s more than just about words and sounds; it’s about reconnecting with the world. With the guidance of skilled speech-language pathologists, adults can overcome their speech limitations and rediscover the power of their voice. This journey may take time, but with persistence and expert help, the results can be life-changing. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of Speech, Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language, reading and writing. She can be reached at kathryn.pengilly@speechinc. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com. S P E E C H , I N C .

articles.text: Paul Nelson, a Piedmont resident of 36 years, published his first book on November 12, entitled Lost Grand Resorts of Old Lake Tahoe. The 224-page book is the culmination of several years of research uncovering the mostly-lost stories of the grand resorts of Lake Tahoe. Nelson unearths the histories of the unique uber-exclusive grand hotels that were built at Lake Tahoe beginning in the 1880s catering to the wealthy owners of California gold mines and Nevada silver mines, and San Francisco society. Most of the stories are not widely known and never have been told in book form. They are enhanced with more than 100 rare historical photos. After setting a contextual background and the resorts’ histories, the book focuses on the lives and exploits of the unique individuals who built and operated them. The central story begins in 1884 with ”Lucky” Baldwin’s fabulous Tallac House (“the world’s grandest hotel”) built on the South Shore of Lake Tahoe. Baldwin was a wealthy and eccentric San Franciscan who built San Francisco’s largest and finest hotel and first grand theater at Powell and Market. Tallac House at Lake Tahoe was operated to great acclaim by the Comstock and Lawrence families for 30 years, with elaborate activities, eight-course French dinners and music by a string quartet. They hired the Maître d’ from the Palace Hotel to give it status. The narrative also follows Tahoe timber baron Duane Bliss, who constructed his ultimate fantasy hotel, the Tahoe Tavern, in Tahoe City, with hundreds of rooms, a theater, bowling alley, restaurants. Later it would become the site of California’s first ski area. New highways built in the 1920s helped bring popularity to Brockway Hotel on Stateline Point with high-end customers including Hollywood celebrities, politicians, mobsters and some of Piedmont’s prominent families. The hotels’ stories are followed through the Depression and World War II up to their ultimate closing and demise in the Lost Grand Resorts of Old Lake Tahoe by Piedmont’s Paul Nelson was published by History Press. 1960s when the taste of tourists moved away from all-inclusive hotels to family cabins, motels and condominiums. Signed first editions of Lost Grand Resorts of Old Lake Tahoe are available by emailing PaulNelsonLaw@gmail.com. The first general release of copies became available online and in bookstores on November 12. Tallac House on Tahoe’s South Shore. Tahoe Tavern in Tahoe City

articles.text: Cory Johnson (right) stands with Dennis Page, owner of SLAM Magazine, which was recently inducted into the Basketball Hall of Fame. Piedmont resident Cory Johnson recently saw a distant dream become a reality. Over 30 years ago in the early 1990s, Johnson became the Founding Editor in Chief of the renowned SLAM Magazine alongside Dennis Page. Being a major piece of the foundation of journalism circling the NBA, SLAM Magazine was inducted into the Basketball Hall of Fame in August, forever holding a piece of professional basketball’s foundation. “It’s super exciting, it’s just so out of the left field bleachers. Dennis and I started the magazine 30 years ago; I went on to do many different things, but Dennis stayed at SLAM Magazine throughout. He told me about their 30th anniversary, then told me the magazine was being inducted and he wanted me to be at the ceremony,” Johnson said. Sitting in a room filled with NBA greatness, Johnson reflects on the night of SLAM’s induction. “Pat Reilly comes in with his wife. Vince Carter and Chauncey Billups were being inducted and were there. Michael Cooper was there and then I look and see James Worthy—then Magic Johnson comes in and says hello. Then Larry Bird comes in, then Dr. J [Julius Erving] comes in, and you’re like holy crap. Then there’s more commotion and in comes Michael Jordan. But the coolest moment of the thing was I was looking at Rick Barry and I notice Dr. J was looking at me and waves. I’m looking around like, do you mean me? Then he waves again and says, ’Yeah, you hi.’ I couldn’t believe he remembered me, it was so cool,” Johnson said. SLAM Magazine was a publication ahead of its time in the world of sports journalism. Instead of the Xs and Os behind sports, they focused on the lesser told story of basketball’s culture rising out of the playgrounds of New York City. It featured hip hop, fashion, and language on the zestier side than what you would find in Sports Illustrated. “The idea was how we would treat language, images, names of the sections, and the pace you’d go through as you read it. In the first issue, we devoted 2-3 pages to Letter to the Editor, and they were all fake letters. No one was reacting to SLAM Magazine yet because we didn’t exist; we just so much wanted to have a connection to the readers. I wanted the readers to be a part of the magazine, just like comic books were for me when I was a kid,” Johnson said. SLAM was a major part of a culture shift in sports in the 90s. They never wanted to act in the traditional sense, which is what Johnson thinks helped propel them to the top of NBA media. “The notion of journalism should be to tell the stories that aren’t being told and to connect with people through those stories. Our goal wasn’t to tell the story of Michael Jordan 50 different ways, the goal was to tell a story of people in the world through the lens of basketball. That meant the playground, high school, and college,” Johnson said. “It’s hard to imagine how racist was American institutions were in the 90s. Over 30 years ago in the early 1990s, Johnson became the Founding Editor in Chief of the renowned SLAM Magazine alongside Dennis Page. He told me about their 30th anniversary, then told me the magazine was being inducted and he wanted me to be at the ceremony,” Johnson said. Sitting in a room filled with NBA greatness, Johnson reflects on the night of SLAM’s induction. “Pat Reilly comes in with his wife. Vince Carter and Chauncey Billups were being inducted and were there. Michael Cooper was there and then I look and see James Worthy—then Magic Johnson comes in and says hello. Then Larry Bird comes in, then Dr. J [Julius Erving] comes in, and you’re like holy crap. Then there’s more commotion and in comes Michael Jordan. But the coolest moment of the thing was I was looking at Rick Barry and I notice Dr. J was looking at me and waves. I’m looking around like, do you mean me? Then he waves again and says, ’Yeah, you hi.’ I couldn’t believe he remembered me, it was so cool,” Johnson said. SLAM Magazine was a publication ahead of its time in the world of sports journalism. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team competed a Chabot College in Hayward in the Western Alameda County Conference Individual Tournament on Friday and Saturday, November 8-9. Juniors Kate Jumper and Arianna Kortum battled their way to the doubles final and finished second to top-seed Juliana Johnson and Sophie Featherstone of Alameda, 6-1, 6-3. Also competing well in the tournament was senior Carolina Romanczuk, who was fourth overall in the singles bracket. Faith Chin finished sixth in singles and Maddie Tran and Emma Chan won the consolation bracket. In doubles. “We had a good WACC League tournament. Carolina took fourth in the singles and Kate and Arianna won a silver in the doubles. Faith also played in the singles winning a round in the main draw and went all the way to the fifth-place finals of the playoffs,” coach Jim Landes said. For Jumper and Kortum, it marked the first time the two paired since their freshman year in 2022. “This is always fun. I’m glad we decided to do this and I hope we get to play again together next year,” Jumper said. “I really enjoy hitting with Kate. The chemistry doesn’t go away because we’re friends off of the court too,” Kortum added. To reach the doubles final, the pair received the No. 2 seed and a first-round bye. They trounced Castro Valley’s Allie Hurka and Abby Wong in the quarterfinals 6-0, 6-2 on Friday and went on to beat Alameda’s No. 3 seed Abby Moore and Zoey Jallen in the semifinals, 6-1, 6-2. In the semifinals, the duo dropped the first game of the first set against Alameda before winning six straight. “I think we just needed to warm up. Once we get past that, we’re fine,” Kortum added. Romanczuk received a firstround bye after being seeded No. 3. In the semifinals, she lost a narrow 7-5, 7-5 match against Sam Lopatin of Berkeley. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team is returning to Witter Field this month with a new coach at the helm, Ben Russell. Hired in September, Russell takes over for the most successful coach in Piedmont High history, Todd Sullivan. “It’s a new group with new coaches and players coming in. We have a wide array of talent and some good freshmen coming into the squad alongside some experienced seniors. It should be a good mix and it’ll be about piecing together the puzzle,” Russell said. Russell comes to Piedmont High with a wealth of experience. He’s been at 24-7 UK Soccer Academy for the past nine years, the same club program that Sullivan coaches. Russell was its technical director from 2015 to 2023, and oversaw Piedmont Soccer Club, giving him a unique familiarity with the school’s student-athletes. “A lot of the players I’ve coached within that nine-year time frame. I think I coached most of these players at some point in their lives. It’s been quite cool from my own personal perspective to touch base with players who I started my journey with 8-9 years ago,” Russell said. Russell, another native of England, began his coaching career in the UK’s professional leagues before coming to the U.S. In addition to coaching at 24-7 he was assistant to Oakland Soccer Club’s men’s and women’s teams which play in the National Premier Soccer League. “I was working out in the Pacific Northwest along with the Canadian region. I wanted to pursue a professional coaching Piedmont High’s boys’ soccer team returns with new head coach Ben Russell at the helm. pathway and did that in England with professional academies like Tottenham, Arsenal, Chelsea and West Ham. But it wasn’t the sustainable lifestyle that I was looking for. I got an opportunity out here with 24-7 and that allowed me to have different experiences with all ages and experiences,” Russell said. Piedmont finished last season with a 12-3-3 record and was the No. 2 seed in the Division 3 North Coast Section postseason. They defeated No. 15 Novato 6-1 in the first round but lost 3-1 to No. 7 Archie Williams in the second round. “The program has had a lot of success and a lot of good players have come through the program, so hopefully we can build from that. Hopefully there’s promise for this year and years to come with young talent coming in,” Russell said. Junior leaders Elles Kreickhaus and goalie Luke McAuliffe, who were members of the 2023 roster, shared their thoughts on how the school’s lack of a pool impacted tournament results. “We only have an hour-long practice sometimes and there was a point where we weren’t in the water at all; running around the Witter track for conditioning. articles.text: The largest and most comprehensive exhibition of American portraitist Amy Sherald’s work to date opens at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) this Saturday, November 16. Georgia-born Sherald is wellknown for her portrayal of prominent African American figures in intimate portraits. The exhibition, entitled American Sublime, features nearly 50 paintings made from 2007 to present, including iconic portraits of Breonna Taylor and former first lady Michelle Obama. In 2018, the artist was selected by the Ms. Obama to paint her portrait as an official commission for the National Portrait Gallery in Washington, D.C. Another highlight of the exhibition is For Love, and for Country (2022), which SFMOMA recently acquired for its permanent collection. “Amy Sherald is one of the most important artists working today and we are honored to present her first mid-career survey at SFMOMA,” Museum Director Christopher Bedford said. “Sherald’s vision deeply resonates with the museum’s goals to share and Artist Amy Sherald to champion a more expansive art history in our galleries. Her unique and exquisite renderings of her subjects encourage close looking, curiosity, and awe.” American Sublime is curated by Sarah Roberts, SFMOMA’s Head of Painting and Sculpture. “Sherald has invented an entirely new form of figurative painting. Her approach goes beyond portraiture to enact new conditions for seeing, feeling, and understanding shared humanity,” Roberts said. “In the spirit of great American artists like Edward Hopper, Alice Neel and Kerry James Marshall, Sherald’s works reframe our understanding of American culture.” Roberts added that Sherald’s portraits “invite viewers to recognize and move beyond preconceived ideas and engage in more expansive thinking about race, representation and the wide-open possibilities and complexities of every individual.” The exhibition will be on display through March 9, 2025. SFMOMA member previews are this Thursday through Saturday, November 14 through 16. Visit https://www.sfmoma.org/ exhibition/amy-sherald-american-sublime/ to learn more.
articles.title: Amy Sherald exhibit opens at SFMOMA on Saturday

articles.text: The Holiday Ice Rink in San Francisco’s Union Square The Holiday Ice Rink in Union Square in San Francisco opened last week and will be open to the public through January 20 for the 17th year. The rink will operate daily from 10 a.m. to 11 p.m., with a planned early closure at 9:30 p.m. on New Year’s Eve, December 31. Tickets are $20 for adults and $15 for children 8 and under, which includes skate rental. All tickets must be purchased in advance at www.unionsquareicerink.com. A portion of ticket proceeds benefits the San Francisco Recreation and Parks Department. “We are excited to showcase all the festive activities and shopping experiences Union Square has to offer while providing a safe and enjoyable environment where everyone can fully immerse themselves in the holiday spirit,” said Marisa Rodriguez, CEO of the Union Square Alliance. The temporary rink is surrounded by festive lights and is adjacent to the iconic Macy’s Christmas Tree, the tallest in San Francisco. For over a decade and a half, the event has drawn guests of all ages, providing a quintessential San Francisco winter experience in the city’s premier shopping plaza. Daily events include a drag performer ice skating show, a silent skate party and “Flashback Fridays.” Sponsors of The Holiday Ice Rink include Safeway, Kaiser Permanente and the American Conservatory Theater. Visit www.unionsquareicerink.com to purchase tickets and to learn more.
articles.title: Union Square ice skating rink opens for holidays

articles.text: Dr. Suess’s greatest children’s stories come to life on the Berkeley Playhouse stage in the whimsical musical Seussical, performing through December 22. Directed by William Thomas Hodgson and choreographed by Leslie Waggoner, the musical is a collection of the writer’s most beloved stories including Cat in the Hat, The Lorax and Horton Hears a Who. “I have such a fondness for this show,” said Berkeley Playhouse Artistic Director Kimberly Dooley. “I directed William in our production of Seussical in 2011 when he performed as Cat in the Hat. It’s an absolute delight to see him come full circle and get to be in the director’s seat.” Dooley added that the characters and cast this year “are zany and vibrant, and there are some really heartfelt moments that leave you feeling inspired.” Some cast members have family members performing, making Suessical “an intergenerational musical,” she said. The cast includes Stephen Kanaski as Cat in the Hat, Christian Arteaga as Horton the Elephant, No’Eau Kahalekulu as Gertrude McFuzz and Andrea Rae as Mayzie La Bird. “This is a family show, it’s a holiday show, it’s a feel-good show, it is a raucous show,” said director Hodgson. Performances run Friday through Sunday and select weekday evenings. For tickets or more information, call the box office at (510) 845-8542 x351 or visit berkeleyplayhouse.org to purchase online. Keenan Moran (Jojo) and Stephen Kanaski (Cat in the Hat) perform in Berkeley Playhouse’s production of Seussical.

articles.text: American Conservatory Theatre (A.C.T) presents the world premiere of A Whynot Christmas Carol, a brand-new take on Charles Dickens’s famous holiday classic. It opens on Tuesday, November 26, with performances through Christmas Eve, December 24 at the Toni Rembi Theater, 415 Geary Street in San Francisco. Award-winning playwright Craig Lucas and Tony Award winner and A.C.T. Artistic Director Pam MacKinnon re envision Dickens’ beloved classic A Christmas Carol as a joyous and comedic new-age play. A Whynot Christmas Carol is about a small theater troupe in the town of Whynot who put on their own holiday play, from first rehearsal to opening night. “A Whynot Christmas Carol brings together everything we love about the season—ghosts, music, magic, humor, and a fresh take on a beloved story that speaks to our times,” said director Pam MacKinnon. “It’s a celebration of the common good and the importance of community that resonates with audiences of all ages in the heart of San Francisco.” The cast, led by Stacy Ross as Aubrei and Dan Hiatt as Phil, includes Catherine Castellanos (Fran), Devin A. Cunningham (Chima), Michelle Drexler (Fran/ Karen Understudy), Rosie Hallett (Karen), Patrick Kelly Jones (Holts), John R. Lewis (Jess/ Chima Understudy), Sarah Toby Moore (Swan), Jenny Nguyen Nelson (Simone), Carrie Paff (Aubrei/Swan Understudy), Gianna DiGregorio Rivera (Lark), Michael Shipley(Holts/ Phil Understudy), Alyssa Leanne So (Simone/Lark Understudy), and Jomar Tagatac (Jess). Set and costume design is by Tony Award winner David Zinn, the costume mastermind behind A.C.T.’s The Wizard of Oz. Choreography is by Erika Chong Shuch. Single tickets are available online at act-sf.org/a-whynotchristmas-carol or by calling the box office at 415-749-2228. All performances are at the 415 Geary Street in San Francisco. articles.text: The San Francisco Symphony will perform Handel’s Messiah, a musical meditation on Christ’s birth, life, and resurrection, on December 6 and 7. Conductor Stephen Stubbs leads the symphony and chorus in this classic holiday favorite. Stubbs is a lutenist and has been a leading figure in the American early music scene for nearly three decades. The performances will feature Amanda Forsy the soprano, John Holiday, countertenor, Aaron Sheehan, tenor, and Douglas Williams, baritone. Davies Symphony Hall will be decorated for the holidays during these performances, filled with lit evergreen trees, and wreaths and garlands. The hall’s lobby bar will feature festive winter cocktails, including a Gingerbread Old Fashioned, sparkling wine and holiday-themed desserts. Performances begin at 7:30 p.m. on Friday and Saturday. Tickets are on sale now. Visit https://www.sfsymphony.org/ Buy-Tickets/2024-25/messiah or call the box office at (415) 864- 6000 to purchase tickets. Soprano Amanda Forsythe

articles.text: The Old Man & the Gun is billed as Robert Redford’s farewell role. And what a wonderful tip of the hat it is. It’s an easygoing, amiable crime comedy of sorts, filled with moments that create a long-lasting smile because it’s so enjoyable. Redford portrays Forrest Tucker, a fedora-wearing oldster who happens to be a bank robber (and a prison escape artist). Set in the early 1980s every frame of the film has an old-time feel to it, most shot in soft sepia tones. The look of it is a perfect fit for Redford. The film opens in a small town inside a small bank. Forest walks up to the manager and with a smile explains that he’s not there for a loan or to make a deposit. He’s there to rob the bank. Flashing his gun in his waistband, he asks politely, still smiling, for the cash on hand. He is so pleasant, so gentlemanly that those he robs describe him in endearing terms. Getting what must be his second or third wind, Forrest cuts a crimespree bank-heist swath across the Southwest. Clearly, he feels more alive, more himself when strolling into and then out of a bank with an old, worn briefcase full of teller cash. On his way home from one “job” he stops to help a woman, Jewel (Sissy Spacek), who is having car trouble. Offering her a ride home, they make a stop for a cup of coffee. And, like everyone else that Forrest meets, she takes a liking Robert Redford stars in The Old Man & the Gun to him. Ditto detective John Hunt (Casey Affleck), who is determined to catch up with not only Forrest but with his two partners in crime (Danny Glover and Tom Waits). What makes this film exceptional is how it moves forward with the audience completely on Forrest’s side. As well, the small ember romance between Jewel and Forrest rings true – from their first coffee shop chat and then, later, when he tells her he’s a bank robber and she laughs and says something to the effect, “Yeah, right.” Perhaps she believes him; however, he is gently likable and good company. articles.text: A scene from Pixar’s Cars 2 What has made Pixar animated feature films so extraordinary is that the Studio clearly understands its audience: kids. Hence the animators and storytellers can let their imaginations rip and the results have been award-winning. The Cars trilogy, beginning with Cars, followed by Cars 2, and Cars 3, are examples. Where the fist Cars is set in the small, sleepy town of Radiator Springs, Cars 2 changes and heads off to Europe where Lightning McQueen (Owen Wilson) intends to enter the World Grand Prix, intent on proving he’s the fastest of the fast. Unexpectedly, he takes with him his bud Tow Truck Mater And so begins a kid friendly journey-adventure that involves lots of action, vroom vroom racing, and to the surprise of youngsters. a detour to London by Tow Truck Mater who gets ensnarled in an espionage plot. He is believed by the bad guys to be a spy disguised as a tow truck. There’s also Finn McMissile (Micharl Caine), good guy spy accompanied by sidekick Holly Shiftwell (Emily Mortimer), and the requisite villain, Professor Zuundapp (Thomas Kretschmann), who is laying plans to sabotage the Grand Prix race using techie stuff such as an electromagnetic generator. It all has a James Bond feel to it with lots of thrills, car chases and high-octane excitement in the mix. Surprisingly, Mater is at the center of the action; however not to forget that McQueen is determined to cross the checker flag finish line first. The action takes place in Italy, Tokyo, and London. articles.text: The Secret Life of Pets is set initially in the New York apartment complex of Katie (Ellie Kemper), who lives with her Jack Russell terrier, Max. But as we soon discover, the building is a menagerie of domesticated pets, and Max, being a gregarious mutt, socializes with his neighbors. There’s Chloe (Lake Bell), an obese, finicky tabby cat; Mel (Bobby Moynihan), a hardcharging pug, Buddy (Hannibal Buress), a likable miniature dachshund; Sweet Pea, a yellow and blue parakeet, and a snowwhite Pomeranian named Gidget (Jenny Slate). The story begins when Katie decides Max could use some company and brings home an oversized, Newfoundland pooch she calls Duke (Eric Stonestreet). Naturally Max and Duke have issues and it’s at this point that the premise of the story is fully revealed. What do the animals do all day while their owners are at work? It is one adventure after another involving lots of New York animals that they meet along the way. Some, such as Snowball (Kevin Hart), are decidedly not domesticated. articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok Anytime Pumpkin Chocolate Snack Bars are easy to make and delicious to eat. Stay with me here, as we jump into the already crowded field of pumpkin-mania. This entry is a keeper though. I knew I was onto a winner when the batter tasted like my pumpkin pie filling, before it’s baked. With an intentional light hand on the spices, there’s plenty of pumpkin flavor. And when highlighted by chocolate chips, you have a classic favorite pairing. The sugar content is dialed down to a mere half cup. The addition of walnuts steer it toward a slightly healthy direction, hence I’ve dubbed these “snack bars” rather than a cookie or cake. The bars are plenty sweet enough to qualify for “treat” status, can be enjoyed anytime. I envision a future batch with a streusel topping to land it into breakfast territory; or a drizzle of melted chocolate to fancy it up a bit. P.S. An easy substitution of mashed, ripe bananas in place of the pumpkin puree is delicious. This idea came to me as I looked at some very speckled bananas on the kitchen counter. Of course then you’ll need to call them Banana Chocolate Snack Bars. Anytime Pumpkin Chocolate Snack Bars Makes one 9x9-inch pan Ingredients 3/4 cup pumpkin puree; canned is fine 1/2 cup granulated sugar 2 large eggs 4 tablespoons unsalted butter, melted and cooled slightly 1/2 teaspoon ground cinnamon 1/4 teaspoon ground ginger 1/4 teaspoon ground nutmeg 1 cup all-purpose flour 1 teaspoon baking powder 1/2 teaspoon salt 1 cup semi-sweet chocolate chips 1 cup walnuts, chopped (optional) Instructions Line a 9 x 9-inch pan with aluminum foil and butter lightly. The easiest way I’ve found to do this neatly is to invert the pan and cover it with a 12 x 12-inch sheet of foil. Carefully fold the corners as if wrapping a gift box. Gently lift the foil off of the pan, turn the pan right-side up, and then tuck the perfectly molded foil neatly into the pan. Place an oven rack in the center of the oven. Preheat the oven to 350° F. Measure the flour, baking powder and salt in a small bowl; stir or whisk to combine. Set aside. Combine the pumpkin and sugar into a large bowl and mix to blend. Either a sturdy hand whisk or electric mixer does the job. Add the eggs, one at a time, and mix well to incorporate into the batter. Add the spices, mixing until they are evenly distributed. Add the butter and mix until smooth. Slowly add the flour mixture and mix until fully incorporated. When the batter is smooth, but not over-mixed, add in the chocolate chips and nuts. Stir to combine well. Spread the batter evenly into the prepared pan. Bake for about 30 minutes, until a toothpick inserted into the center of the pan comes out clean. Cool on a wire rack for at least 20 minutes before cutting. Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on November 2, 2016

The sizes, composition, and detailing of the openings are one of the most important design considerations in determining the style and quality of the architecture. The early high-rise buildings in the late 1800’s were equipped, for example, with residential style double hung windows. Some of these can still be seen in old downtown San Francisco office buildings but would be completely aesthetically and functionally unacceptable in a new high-rise building today. Glazing (the actual glass of the window) has itself evolved vastly over the last couple of centuries. In the old days, window sizes were limited by glass sizes. The invention of flat glass made large glass sheets possible and gave a new freedom to fenestration design. This used to be plate glass, which is characterized by imperfections and slight “wave” distortion as you look through it. Nowadays, pretty much all glazing is float glass. It is named for the manufacturing process which includes floating the glass over molten tin. Only developed in the 1950’s, it is of a uniform thickness and has the even, clear appearance we are most familiar with today. Since up to 70% of energy loss of a building is through the fenestration, high energy-efficient windows are required and used everywhere in our era. They include the familiar double (or even triple) glazing, and low E glass coatings. I have found that one of the most difficult parts of building design is to make the overall exterior composition of the fenestration jibe with the requirements of the interior rooms. In other words, the fenestration has to work both inside and out, visually and functionally. In addition to considering the proportions and light and ventilation of each interior room, certain windows (in bedrooms) have to be sized to meet emergency exit requirements to allow occupants escape and firefighters egress. Another important building code requirement that enters into fenestration design is the requirement for tempered glass. Tempered glass is stronger, but more importantly, breaks into small granular chunks instead of dangerous dagger-like shards, as does normal glass. All glass in doors, and windows adjacent to doors, is now required to be tempered glass. Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. McNamara graduated from Piedmont High School in 1933 He was one of the school’s brightest pupils, but the Depression left his family little money for his further education. However, he discovered tuition at the University of California in Berkeley, would cost only $52 a year, and he graduated in 1937 with a B.A. in economics with minors in mathematics and philosophy. He got a master’s degree from Harvard Business School and became an accountant with Price Waterhouse. He later joined Harvard’s faculty. Poor eyesight kept McNamara from military service during World War II, but he volunteered to train air force staff. After the war, he joined nine of his military colleagues as a team offering management expertise to companies. Henry Ford II hired them, and they successfully reorganized Ford Motor Co. McNamara rose steadily and became the first non-member of the Ford family to become the company’s president. After John F Kennedy was elected President, he offered McNamara his choice of being either Secretary of Treasury or Defense. He chose Defense. McNamara became increasingly embroiled in the Vietnam War. Kennedy believed that America’s reputation would be undermined if it seemed unwilling to protect a small Asian nation from communism. By the time of Kennedy’s assassination in 1963 there were 10,000 American “advisers” in South Vietnam, and America became mired deeply in the conflict. The anti-war movement swelled, and protesters began to dub the conflict “McNamara’s war.” However, McNamara became disenchanted with the war and in November 1967 he expressed his reservations in a confidential memorandum to President Johnson. Four weeks later Johnson announced McNamara’s election as president of the World Bank and his departure from the Defense Department. articles.text: Nancy McDaniel, a former professional golfer and head coach of the Cal women’s golf team for 29 years, died in Oakland, California on October 23, 2024, her home for 30 years, after a courageous battle with breast cancer. Born Nancy Kessler in Portland, Oregon on November 9, 1966, she was the daughter of Donald and Marilyn Kessler and the youngest of five children. Nancy grew up in Portland, and sports were always in her life, starting early. She played basketball for LaSalle High School and in her senior year helped lead the team to a high school state championship. Nancy herself earned first-team all-state honors. Golf however was the sport that played the biggest part in Nancy’s life – she was a player, coach, a volunteer, and the wife of Jay McDaniel, a PGA head golf professional. Nancy started golf at a young age, playing and winning junior golf tournaments in Oregon. She competed for the University of Washington golf team from 1984 to 1988, and was the Husky women’s golf team captain, a collegiate All-American, and was chosen for the Pac- 10 All-Decade Team. After college, Nancy played professionally for five years, but left tour golf to create the University of California women’s golf team in Berkeley, where she was the head coach for 29 seasons. While there, she led the Golden Bears to 10 NCAA Championship appearances, 22 NCAA regional appearances, and two conference championships. Nancy’s contributions to the game of golf were recognized by her inductions into the National College Golf Coaches Hall of Fame and the Cal Athletics Hall of Fame. Nancy was also recently inducted into the Northern California Golf Association Hall of Fame. To those who knew her as “coach,” Nancy will be rememtaking a hike with friends. Being a mom and a wife were at the core of Nancy’s being, and she was devoted to her husband Jay and her children, Tyler and Molly. Nancy will be remembered as quick to laugh, always positive, direction-oriented, clear in what she thought, and full of energy and strength. Those who knew her will not forget the fun, light, warmth and humor she brought into every room. Her determination and courage in the face of adversity were an inspiration not only to her family but to everyone who knew her. Although she always projected strength, her capacity for love ran deep. Nancy will be greatly missed. Nancy is survived by her husband Jay McDaniel, and children Tyler and Molly of Oakland, as well as her siblings Ann Culhane, David Kessler, and Scott Kessler, and her uncle Kurt Kessler. She was preceded in death by her parents and brother, Thomas Kessler. A mass will be held for Nancy at St. Theresa Church, 30 Mandalay Road, Oakland, on Friday, November 15th, at 11 a.m. Following the mass, a Celebration of Life will begin at 1 p.m. at The Claremont Country Club in Oakland. Please note and observe Claremont’s dress code policy (https://claremontcountryclub. com/dress-code-policy). In lieu of flowers, the McDaniel family request donations to two organizations in Nancy’s honor: Play for Her, to support the fight against breast cancer (https://app.99pledges. com /f u nd /2024play forher), and The University of California Women’s golf team for the Nancy McDaniel Legacy Fund (https://give.berkeley.edu/fund/ FU0754000).
